science.title: The complexity paradox of generalist AI agents in medicine: exploring GPT-5 for real-world multimodal medical diagnosis
science.description: The next generation of medical AI systems that integrate language understanding, web data retrieval, and multi-step reasoning are demonstrating increasing promise as potential diagnostic aids in technical evaluations. However, their real world diagnostic performance, explainability, and reliability remain unclear. We conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician validated real world cases. Each model was assessed for diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration, and robustness to low-quality inputs. We found important limitations in these AI systems, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Yet the models also showed strengths, including effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval. To support clinical deployment and future model development, we recommend prioritizing reasoning-optimized AI models, improving information retrieval mechanisms for reflection and error correction, strengthening visual-textual integration, and establishing practical standards for image quality and clarity. Overall, reliable real world multimodal diagnostic performance depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows. Persistent gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to safe routine clinical use.

science.title: Design and validation of a questionnaire to measure competency development in VR‑supported undergraduate physiology labs
science.description: This study reports the design and validation of a self-report questionnaire to assess transversal competencies associated with the use of Virtual Reality (VR) in higher education. The instrument was developed and used in an undergraduate physiology course, where VR-supported laboratory sessions enabled students to explore four physiological systems: gas transport, cardiovascular function, muscle contraction, and renal function and micturition. Rather than measuring content-specific learning, the questionnaire targets four transversal competencies that immersive learning environments may foster: conceptual understanding, evidence-informed decision-making, information and communication technology (ICT) operation, and application to practice. Instrument development followed a multi-phase validation procedure comprising expert judgment using Aiken’s V, a pilot study with 322 students, and a final psychometric analysis with a refined 26-item instrument administered to a validation sample of 58 students. The questionnaire demonstrated excellent sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.966) and internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.993). Exploratory Factor Analysis identified a four-factor solution accounting for 76.7% of total variance, and Confirmatory Factor Analysis supported the structural model with acceptable fit indices (CFI = 0.903; TLI = 0.891; RMSEA = 0.086). All factors showed high composite reliability (CR > 0.89) and average variance extracted above the 0.50 threshold, supporting convergent validity. Discriminant validity was confirmed through HTMT ratios below 0.85 across all construct pairs. This study validates the questionnaire exclusively within the Physiology educational lab context in which it was developed. The evidence reported supports score-based inferences about transversal competency development in that setting. Any use of the instrument in other disciplines or institutions should be supported by independent psychometric validation in those contexts.
